summary.text: The Ciconian women — Maenads maddened by Dionysus — who slew Orpheus because he shunned their love after Eurydice, drowning his lyre with tambourines and tearing him apart when his song could no longer protect him.

story.text: Apollodorus says simply that the Maenads tore Orpheus in pieces — the closing act of a life that had already descended to Hades for love and discovered the mysteries of Dionysus.

Ovid names them Ciconian matrons on a hill, breasts concealed in skins of forest animals, who watched the bard who had rejected every woman since Eurydice. Stones and spears hurled at him fell harmless before his harmony; only when pipes, horns, tambourines, and Bacchanalian yells drowned his voice did the stones run red with Thracian blood.

They slew the harmless bard while his outstretched hands implored mercy — the first and only time his voice persuaded no one. Bacchus would not leave the crime unpunished: the Edonian women who had killed his bard sank into the earth, toes rooting to oak as they struggled to flee.
